title: Explore
text:
The Shiny app below lets you interactively explore the two key relationships that underpin the instrumental variables design:

First stage (left panel): Does more rainfall predict greater distance from protests?
Reduced form (right panel): Does more rainfall predict lower turnout?

If both relationships hold, and if the exclusion restriction is credible, then the ratio of the reduced-form to the first-stage coefficient gives the causal effect of protest proximity on turnout.
Use the controls to highlight specific counties, adjust the smoother bandwidth, and toggle spatial outliers. The F-statistic and implied IV ratio update live.



   








Note



Local preview: Clone the repository and run shiny::runApp("shiny/") in R to explore the app without deployment. The app requires processed data from data/processed/ — run scripts 01 through 04 first.

title: Explore
text:
What to Look For
First stage (instrument relevance): A negative, statistically significant slope means rainfall → farther from protests. The F-statistic should exceed 10.
Reduced form (intention-to-treat): A negative slope means higher rainfall → lower turnout. If both slopes are negative and significant, the IV estimate (their ratio) is positive — protests increased turnout.
Spatial outliers: Block groups flagged as spatial outliers (high-leverage in the Moran’s I sense) deserve attention. If the IV result is driven entirely by spatially autocorrelated units, that is a robustness concern.

title: Explore
text:
Future Interactive Components
Two additional apps are planned as the analysis scales nationally:
Protest & Turnout Map Explorer — A Leaflet map of Georgia block groups colored by user-selected variable (turnout / distance / rainfall / IV residuals), with click-to-popup for individual block group data.
Treatment Effect Heterogeneity — After fitting a Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), a choropleth of local 2SLS coefficients will show where in Georgia the protest effect is strongest, alongside a histogram of the coefficient distribution.

title: Methods
text:
The goal is to estimate the causal effect of proximity to a Black Lives Matter protest on 2020 general election turnout at the census block group level in Georgia. Proximity is measured as the straight-line distance (miles) from a block group’s centroid to the nearest 2020 BLM protest event.


Simple OLS regression of turnout on distance is biased because protest locations are not randomly assigned. Protests clustered in urban, high-resource, high-turnout areas — any positive correlation between protest proximity and turnout may reflect pre-existing demographic differences rather than a protest effect.



We use rainfall on protest days as an instrumental variable for protest exposure. The logic:

Relevance: Rain reduces protest size and attendance. Block groups with more rainfall during the protest period were, on average, farther from large protests.
Exclusion: Rainfall on protest days (months before Election Day) has no direct path to November turnout — it operates only through its effect on protest size and location.

This gives us a valid instrument if we are willing to assume that rainfall patterns in May–September 2020 are unrelated to block-group–level political mobilization independent of the protests themselves.

title: Methods
text:
Formal Model

First Stage
\log(\text{dist}_i + 1) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \log(\text{rainfall}_i + 1) + \alpha_2 \text{pop\_dens}_i + \alpha_3 \text{pct\_black}_i + \nu_i
where \hat{\text{dist}}_i (fitted values) is the instrument. The F-statistic on excluded instruments must exceed 10 for the instrument to be considered strong.


Second Stage (2SLS)
\text{turnout}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \widehat{\text{dist}}_i + \sum_t \gamma_t \text{turnout}_{it} + \varepsilon_i
\beta_1 is the causal estimate of interest: the effect of being one mile farther from a protest on block group turnout share.


Reduced Form
\text{turnout}_i = \delta_0 + \delta_1 \log(\text{rainfall}_i + 1) + \sum_t \gamma_t \text{turnout}_{it} + \eta_i
The ratio \hat\delta_1 / \hat\alpha_1 gives the Wald (IV) estimate, which should match the 2SLS coefficient.

title: Methods
text:
Spatial Autocorrelation
Census block groups that are geographically close to each other tend to have similar turnout rates — a violation of the OLS independence assumption. We quantify this with Moran’s I, a spatially-weighted correlation coefficient:
I = \frac{n}{S_0} \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
where w_{ij} is the spatial weight between units i and j (queen contiguity, row-standardized) and S_0 = \sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}.

Spatial Model Specification
Lagrange multiplier (LM) tests on the baseline OLS model indicate non-independent error terms arising from both spatial lag and spatial error processes. We therefore estimate a spatial error model:
\text{turnout}_i = X_i \beta + u_i, \quad u_i = \lambda \sum_j w_{ij} u_j + \varepsilon_i
which absorbs spatially structured unobservables into the error term, producing consistent coefficient estimates. For the IV setting, we use the predicted distance from the first stage as the treatment in the spatial error framework — a practical implementation of the spatial 2SLS approach outlined in Betz, Cook & Hollenbach (2019).

title: Do Black Lives Matter Protests Increase Voter Turnout?
text:
Did the wave of Black Lives Matter protests following George Floyd’s murder in May 2020 causally increase voter turnout in the 2020 presidential election? This project estimates that effect at the census block group level in Georgia, using rainfall on protest days as an instrumental variable for protest exposure.
The core challenge is selection bias: protests occurred disproportionately in urban, high-turnout areas, making naive comparisons misleading. Rainfall is a credible instrument — it plausibly deterred protest attendance without directly affecting who voted on Election Day (months later).

title: Do Black Lives Matter Protests Increase Voter Turnout?
text:
Key Finding

Instrumental variables estimates suggest that proximity to a BLM protest increased block group–level turnout in Georgia’s 2020 general election, even after correcting for spatial autocorrelation in both the outcome and the instrument. OLS estimates of this effect are likely upward-biased due to endogenous protest location.

title: Results
text:
Instrument Validity: Wu-Hausman Test
The Wu-Hausman test evaluates whether OLS is actually inconsistent — i.e., whether distance is truly endogenous. A small p-value rejects the null that OLS and IV estimates are equivalent, supporting the use of IV.


Wu-Hausman test statistic: **6.638** (p = 0.0100)

title: Results
text:
Spatial Autocorrelation in Residuals
If OLS residuals are spatially clustered, standard errors are underestimated and inference is unreliable. The maps below compare OLS vs. 2SLS residuals — spatial structure in residuals signals remaining spatial dependence not captured by the model.





Left: OLS residuals. Right: 2SLS residuals. Remaining spatial clustering in OLS residuals motivates the spatial error specification.







Left: OLS residuals. Right: 2SLS residuals. Remaining spatial clustering in OLS residuals motivates the spatial error specification.

Results from these tests determine whether to use a spatial lag model (missing spatially-lagged DV), a spatial error model (non-independent errors), or a Spatial Durbin model (both). Both lag and error statistics are significant, suggesting a Spatial Durbin specification is appropriate for the final model — a direction for future work.

title: Results
text:
Robustness
The following checks help assess the sensitivity of results:

Alternative control sets: Using only 2018 turnout vs. all five prior election years
Log vs. level distance: log(dist + 1) vs. dist in miles — addresses right-skew
County fixed effects: absorb county-level unobservables (requires sufficient within-county variation in rainfall)

These robustness specifications can be added to R/04-models.R following the established pipeline pattern.
